title: OO design and Clean ABAP
intro: Explain object orientation through responsibilities, replaceable dependencies, and observable behavior. Memorized definitions become useful when you can name a concrete tradeoff. The examples are hypothetical design exercises, not claims about personal project experience; project naming conventions are separate from the SAP language.

questions.question: Explain abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism with one example.
questions.answer: Abstraction gives callers a simple operation, such as send, without showing every technical step. Encapsulation keeps an object in a valid state by controlling access to its data. Inheritance lets a subclass specialize a base class while keeping its promises. Polymorphism lets the same call use different implementations, such as an email sender or a test sender.
questions.detail:
An approval coordinator needs to notify a user. It calls send through a notification interface and supplies a message. The production implementation sends email, while a test implementation records the message for an assertion. The coordinator does not need to know which concrete class it received.

The sender protects its own valid setup, such as a required destination, rather than exposing every attribute for arbitrary changes. If inheritance is used, a subclass must still behave as a valid sender. These ideas work together: callers see a small useful operation, implementation details stay inside the sender, and a new delivery method can be added without rewriting the approval decision.
questions.pitfall: Encapsulation means protecting valid behavior and state, not merely generating getters and setters for every attribute.

questions.question: What can an ABAP interface contain, and when would you use one?
questions.answer: An ABAP interface describes what an implementing class provides. It can contain methods, types, constants, attributes and events, not just method names. I use a small interface when callers need one clear capability and different implementations can provide it. This also lets a test supply a controlled replacement. Specialized interfaces, such as BAdI interfaces, can have additional rules.
questions.detail:
A checkout needs a price, so its price-provider interface can define how to request one and what happens when no price is available. One class reads local data; another calls an external service. The checkout uses the same operation, while the implementations keep their technical work private.

The contract must include behavior as well as types. Returning an empty price on network failure is different from reporting that no price exists. I avoid putting unrelated operations into the interface simply because one concrete class already has them. A narrow interface makes both the caller and its test double easier to understand, and it reduces the effect of future changes.
questions.pitfall: An interface is not an abstract class, and a collection of similarly named methods alone does not establish a meaningful common contract.

questions.question: How do ABSTRACT and FINAL affect classes and methods?
questions.answer: An abstract class cannot be created directly, but it may contain working shared code. It does not have to contain an abstract method. An abstract method leaves implementation to a subclass before that subclass can be concrete. FINAL on a class prevents subclasses. FINAL on a method prevents further redefinition of that method.
questions.detail:
A document-processing base class could provide common logging while leaving a processing step abstract. A concrete subclass implements that step and can then be instantiated if no abstract methods remain. This is useful only when the shared process and the allowed variation are deliberate parts of the design.

For a service that should not be specialized through inheritance, FINAL makes that limit explicit. It can still implement interfaces and receive other objects as dependencies. I follow ABAP rules rather than copying assumptions from another language: redefining an inherited method preserves its interface, and ABAP does not solve this with same-name methods that have different parameter lists.
questions.pitfall: Do not import another language's virtual keyword or method-overloading rules into ABAP; use ABAP's actual redefinition and signature rules.

questions.question: How do upcasting and downcasting work in ABAP Objects?
questions.answer: Upcasting uses a general reference type for an object, such as its superclass or interface. Downcasting asks to use a more specific type. Neither creates a new object. A downcast fails if the actual object does not support the requested type, so I check it or handle CX_SY_MOVE_CAST_ERROR. Frequent downcasts can mean the caller needs a better interface.
questions.detail:
A payment-interface reference can point to a card-payment object. Through that reference, I can use operations declared by the interface. If I really need a card-specific operation, a valid downcast exposes it, but the reference still points to the same object with the same state.

If the reference actually points to a bank-transfer implementation, casting it to the card class cannot turn it into a card. The cast fails. I test that path when a cast is necessary. More often, if ordinary payment processing keeps checking concrete classes, I move the shared capability into a suitable interface so callers can work without knowing every implementation.
questions.pitfall: Casting a reference changes the accessible static view, not the object's dynamic type or stored data.

questions.question: What is the difference between instance and static methods and constructors?
questions.answer: An instance method works with a particular object and its data. A static method belongs to the class and has no current object of its own. The instance constructor prepares a newly created object. The class constructor prepares class-level state when the runtime first needs the class in that internal session. I keep that hidden initialization small and predictable.
questions.detail:
Two approval-service objects can each hold a different repository reference. Their instance methods use their own repository. A static helper, by contrast, cannot assume that either object is its current instance. Class-level data can be shared by those instances within the internal session, so changing it may affect both.

I use the instance constructor to receive required dependencies and establish a usable object. I avoid loading large datasets or calling remote systems unexpectedly from a class constructor. Also, declaring CLASS-METHODS does not itself prevent object creation. Creation visibility or an abstract class controls that, and class data is not automatically one shared value across the whole SAP system.
questions.pitfall: ABAP does not make a class uninstantiable simply because it has static methods, and class data is not automatically shared system-wide.

questions.question: When do you prefer composition over inheritance?
questions.answer: I prefer composition when one object needs help from another: the service has a repository or a formatter. Those helpers can change independently. Inheritance fits a real specialization where the subclass keeps the base class promises. I do not build a class hierarchy just to reuse a few methods. Composition often makes testing and replacing a dependency simpler.
questions.detail:
A report service reads data, checks access and formats output. It can receive a repository, an authorization policy and a formatter as separate helpers. A test replaces the repository while using the real calculation. A new output format does not require a new version of the entire report hierarchy.

A large base report class may instead force every subclass to inherit database, output and security decisions it does not need. That makes a small change affect unrelated reports. I use inheritance when a shared process and its extension steps are genuinely stable. The practical test is whether a subclass can be used wherever the base type is expected without surprising its caller.
questions.pitfall: Code reuse alone is weak justification for inheritance; a subclass that violates caller expectations is not a sound substitute.

questions.question: How do dependency injection and dependency inversion differ?
questions.answer: Dependency inversion means business code depends on the capability it needs, usually an interface, rather than one technical implementation. Dependency injection means someone else supplies that implementation, often through the constructor. The first is a design rule; the second is a way to connect objects. Together they make dependencies visible and easier to replace in tests.
questions.detail:
An approval service needs to read a request. It accepts a repository interface in its constructor instead of creating a database repository inside approve. Production setup supplies the real repository; a unit test supplies a fake that returns a known request. The approval rule itself runs unchanged in both cases.

Passing an object is not enough if the service ignores it and creates another dependency internally. Also, injecting a large concrete database class can still leave business code dependent on database details. I keep the required operations small and meaningful, and test both successful reads and failures through that interface. This reveals what the service really relies on.
questions.pitfall: Injecting a concrete class everywhere may aid construction while still leaving the business layer tightly coupled to infrastructure.

questions.question: How would you apply SOLID without overengineering?
questions.answer: I use SOLID to keep changes understandable. A class should have a clear job, and new variations should not require editing every caller. Replacements should keep the same promises, interfaces should contain what their callers need, and business rules should depend on useful abstractions. I add structure for a real need. More classes do not automatically mean better design.
questions.detail:
A tax calculation mixed with database reads and printing is difficult to test. Separating the calculation lets me give it known values and check the result without a printer or live database. A narrow rate-provider interface may help if rates can come from different places or the source can fail.

That does not mean every five-line helper needs its own interface and factory. I ask which change or test becomes easier because of each extra layer. Single responsibility does not mean exactly one method per class. Open/closed also does not forbid fixing existing code; it encourages a design where expected variations can be added without repeatedly disrupting stable business logic.
questions.pitfall: Single responsibility does not mean one method per class, and open/closed does not mean existing code must never be changed.

questions.question: When are Strategy and Factory useful?
questions.answer: Strategy puts different versions of a rule behind the same interface. A factory chooses and creates objects so callers do not need to know their setup. They can work together: a factory selects a country-specific pricing strategy. I use only as much structure as needed. A static creation helper is a simple factory, not automatically the formal Factory Method pattern.
questions.detail:
A coordinator calculates prices for domestic and export orders. It receives a pricing strategy and asks it to calculate using explicit order data. The coordinator keeps the common workflow, while each strategy contains its own rule. Tests run the same coordinator with both strategies and verify the results.

If configuration determines the choice, a factory can validate that configuration and build the right strategy. An unknown value should produce a useful error, not silently select a rule that could charge the wrong price. When only one straightforward implementation exists, direct construction at the application entry point may be enough. The pattern should remove confusion, not introduce a hierarchy without a need.
questions.pitfall: Do not call every method that returns an object Factory Method without distinguishing a simple factory from the formal pattern.

questions.question: What do Adapter and Facade solve in SAP integration code?
questions.answer: An Adapter translates between two interfaces. A Facade gives callers one simple operation over a process with several steps. For a legacy posting API, an adapter can map fields and errors, while a facade coordinates prepare, check and post. Both must keep commit rules, authorization and failure behavior visible. A wrapper does not make an unreleased API safe for ABAP Cloud.
questions.detail:
The application has a simple posting request, but a function module expects several technical structures. An adapter translates those structures and converts the response into useful application errors. A facade can then offer one submit operation that runs the required steps in the right order and stops when checking fails.

I still inspect whether the underlying API commits internally or has a separate save step. Hiding that fact could leave a partial result when the caller expects rollback. Tests should cover field mapping, rejected checks and uncertain remote results. The wrapper also keeps its original SAP dependencies; adding a clean interface alone does not make those dependencies released or Clean Core Level A.
questions.pitfall: Wrapping an unreleased SAP object does not by itself make that underlying dependency released, cloud compliant, or clean-core Level A.

questions.question: What are the limitations of Singleton in ABAP?
questions.answer: A Singleton normally returns one stored object within an ABAP internal session. It is not one object for every user or application server. Shared mutable data can leak between operations and tests, and replacing the singleton can be difficult. I use it only when its lifetime is intentional. An explicitly supplied shared service is often easier to control.
questions.detail:
A singleton caches configuration after the first read. Another operation changes the configuration, but the cached object still returns the old value. Creating a new caller does not necessarily refresh that singleton. Tests can show the same problem: one test changes shared state and a later test unexpectedly sees it.

I define how the cache is keyed, when it expires and who may clear it. If no long-lived shared state is needed, I create a service for the operation and pass it to callers. A singleton is also not a locking mechanism. Separate sessions can each hold their own instance, so it cannot by itself prevent two users from changing the same business object.
questions.pitfall: A singleton does not synchronize business updates across sessions, work processes, application servers, or users.

questions.question: How do ABAP OO events differ from durable business events?
questions.answer: An ABAP OO event calls registered handlers in the current runtime context. It is useful for local notifications, such as a UI interaction. A durable business event must survive failures and support delivery after the business change is saved. That needs a supported event or integration mechanism. RAISE EVENT alone does not provide persistence, retry or reliable external delivery.
questions.detail:
An ALV can raise a local event when the user selects a row. A controller registered with SET HANDLER reacts and updates the display. If that session ends, the local event is not a saved message waiting for another system. This is appropriate for an immediate screen interaction.

Starting an external approval workflow after a document is saved is a different requirement. The design must coordinate save and publication, identify duplicates, monitor failed delivery and support retries. Otherwise the workflow could start for a document that later fails to save, or never start after a temporary outage. Similar event terminology does not make the two delivery mechanisms interchangeable.
questions.pitfall: RAISE EVENT by itself does not persist a message or guarantee workflow creation after a commit.

questions.question: What would you change first in a difficult legacy ABAP method?
questions.answer: I first find out what the method promises to its callers and who owns its save. Then I make small changes: clearer names, less duplication and separate calculation from database or remote calls. I protect risky behavior with focused tests before larger changes. The goal is easier understanding without changing the business result accidentally.
questions.detail:
A long posting method calculates a discount, reads configuration and saves a document. I first extract the discount calculation if its inputs and result can be made clear. I leave commit, authorization and locking behavior in place until I understand their callers and tests. That gives reviewers a small change they can verify.

Next I use tests around important amounts, rejection paths and existing edge cases before moving more code. Merely converting every loop into an expression can obscure the actual change. Team naming also helps consistency: this project uses lt_ for tables, ls_ for structures and co_ for constants. Those are project conventions, not special ABAP syntax or universal Clean ABAP requirements.
questions.pitfall: A broad stylistic rewrite without behavior evidence can introduce regressions and make review harder, even if the result looks more modern.

questions.question: How do you make an OO design testable, and what should ABAP Unit assert?
questions.answer: I keep the business rule real and make outside dependencies replaceable. Tests supply known data, time or service responses and check the result a caller can observe. I cover normal cases, limits and failures. Coverage can reveal untested code, but it cannot prove the assertions are useful. Real database, authorization and service behavior still need integration checks.
questions.detail:
An approval rule sends amounts above a limit to a manager. I test below, exactly at and above that limit, plus the case where no manager is available. A repository double supplies the request, and the test checks the real decision and reported error. The expected result comes from the rule, not from repeating the implementation in the test.

I also simulate a read failure so it cannot become an accidental approval. Separate tests in the target environment verify the actual repository and security behavior. A unit test with fake persistence is valuable, but it cannot prove a real service call, save or role assignment works correctly.
questions.pitfall: A test that only asserts that a method returned, or mirrors its implementation step by step, provides weak evidence.

questions.question: How does MVC separate responsibilities?
questions.answer: The Model holds application data and relevant behavior. The View displays information and accepts user input. The Controller handles interactions and coordinates what happens next. MVC separates these jobs so changes are easier to manage. It does not require one fixed call sequence, and it does not move backend business rules into the browser.
questions.detail:
In a SAPUI5 application, a view binds a list to a model. When a user presses Submit, the controller gathers the intended action and calls the backend. The backend checks the business rules and permissions, then returns success or an error. The model and bindings help the screen reflect the result.

A disabled Submit button is useful feedback, but it cannot be the only enforcement of the rule. Someone can call the service directly. I keep required validation in the backend and use the UI for a clear experience. This division also helps testing: a controller interaction test and a backend business-rule test prove different parts of the application.
questions.pitfall: MVC does not mean copying all backend business logic into the UI controller or assuming the view must always be manually rebuilt.
